title: Revisiting Private Credit’s Next Stress Test
summary: LPL Research examines private credit and the refinancing, underwriting, and AI risks that could drive the market’s next stress test.

# Revisiting Private Credit’s Next Stress Test


[Lawrence Gillum](https://www.lpl.com/research/research-team/lawrence-gillum.html) | Chief Fixed Income Strategist


Last Updated: November 17, 2026


## Revisiting Private Credit’s Next Stress Test


Earlier this year, several high-profile credit problems put private credit under the microscope. The headlines have since quieted, but that should not be confused with an all clear. In a recent conversation with Matt Pallai, CIO of Private Credit at Nomura Asset Management International, we revisited the risks and opportunities across the market.


One encouraging development is that corporate private credit conditions have not deteriorated as much as some feared. Default pressures appear to have plateaued or improved modestly, while healthier companies generally continue to refinance. The bigger adjustment may simply be accepting that borrowing costs could remain higher than they were during the post-financial crisis era. For weaker borrowers, however, elevated payment-in-kind interest and other forms of restructuring suggest stress has not disappeared.


Technology is another important fault line and was a large contributor to the headline risk earlier in the year. Software and technology represent more than 20% of some measures of corporate direct lending, leaving investors potentially more exposed to artificial intelligence (AI) disruption than they realize. Meanwhile, the enormous AI infrastructure buildout is creating new lending opportunities but also new risks. As Matt highlighted, debt investors capture far less upside than equity investors while remaining exposed to uncertain cash flows, technological obsolescence, refinancing risk, and potentially longer regulatory timelines for data center projects.


That makes diversification increasingly important. Private credit extends well beyond corporate direct lending into real estate, asset-backed finance, specialty finance, and other areas. Matt was particularly constructive on asset-backed lending, where loans can be supported by identifiable collateral and opportunities such as equipment finance, healthcare lending, and other specialty assets can provide return streams less connected to the economic forces driving traditional corporate credit.


Importantly, neither of us sees private credit as another 2008-style systemic threat. Leverage is generally lower and financing structures better match the duration of underlying assets. But private credit remains credit. A meaningful economic slowdown would likely bring higher defaults and losses.


The takeaway for the next 18 months is straightforward: vigilance, diversification, and conservative underwriting. As higher rates work through the economy, those disciplines should increasingly separate stronger managers and strategies from the rest.


For a deeper discussion, tune in to this week’s[LPL Market Signals podcast](https://www.lpl.com/research/market-signals-podcast/revisiting-private-credits-next-stress-test.html) , where Matt and I discuss where the next stress points may emerge and what could separate the winners from the losers.
